title: Divorce, permitted not loved
hook: permitted but disliked, with waiting periods and kindness

segments.voice: Yesterday, rights in marriage: kindness, provision, consultation, dignity, and spouses as raiment for each other. Your line was rights both ways. What did you quietly take off someone's hands? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

A woman comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about her husband, Thabit ibn Qays. And she starts by defending him. I don't fault him, she says, not his character and not his faith. But she can't stay. She's afraid that if she stays, she'll fall short of what she owes in the marriage. The Prophet doesn't lecture her. He asks one practical question: will you give him back his garden? The garden was his gift to her. Yes, she says. So he tells Thabit to take the garden back and let her go. In Sahih al-Bukhari, a marriage ends without a villain. Today's word: talaq.
screen: `I DON'T FAULT HIM.` → `WILL YOU GIVE BACK HIS GARDEN?` → `A MARRIAGE ENDS WITHOUT A VILLAIN.`

segments.voice: Talaq is divorce, and in Islamic law the husband's release of the marriage. First, its place. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud says that of the things Allah has permitted, the one He dislikes most is divorce. Hadith scholars have debated its chain. Some readers hear the same idea in the verses themselves: a door that exists, and is not meant to be swung lightly. Second, what comes before it. Surah four says that when a breach is feared between husband and wife, an arbiter is to be appointed from his family and an arbiter from hers, and if they want to set things right, Allah will bring them together. Talk first, with people who love both sides. Third, how the door is built. Surah two, in Pickthall's translation: "Divorce must be pronounced twice and then (a woman) must be retained in honour or released in kindness." Each of those first two times, there is a waiting period, and during it the couple can come back together. There's room to cool off and change course. And at the end, whichever way it goes, kindness. The same verse forbids taking back what was given to her, with one exception. Fourth, that exception, the wife's door. That's the story from the hook. When the wife asks to leave and returns the gift, it has its own name, khul'. Divorce isn't only something done to her. She can seek her release too. The schools differ on details, including what happens when someone says the word three times at once. But the shape holds. Permitted, because sometimes a marriage can't go on. Not loved, because it's still a breaking. And even the breaking has manners.
screen: `PERMITTED, BUT DISLIKED.` · `AN ARBITER FROM EACH FAMILY.` · `TWICE, WITH TIME TO RETURN.` · `SHE CAN SEEK HER RELEASE, TOO.` · then, large: `RELEASED IN KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: The practice: end things kindly. Breathe in, and out, slowly. Bring to mind something that has ended for you, or needs to: a friendship, a job, a habit, a group you've outgrown, or something larger. Don't go over the whole story. Just ask: could I leave it without making the other side a villain? Is there something of theirs I should give back, a word of thanks, an apology, an honest goodbye? Let one kind sentence form in your mind. You don't have to send it. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for gentleness in endings. The bell holds the time.
Talaq. Divorce in Islam: permitted but disliked, with arbiters first, waiting periods, a way back, and parting in kindness. Today's word.
Your line: permitted, not loved. Today, if something has to end, a plan, a conversation, a commitment, end it without making anyone the villain. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Muslim couples in difficulty are encouraged to seek reconciliation, for example through family members or an imam, before divorce; a divorce is followed by a waiting period during which the couple may reconcile, and a wife may seek a release of her own, called khul'.

fork.setup: a woman tells the Prophet she has no complaint about her husband's character or faith, but she can't stay. what does he do?
options: tell her she has no reason, so she must stay.
ask if she'll give back the garden he gave her.
send her husband away in disgrace.
fork.reveal: she agreed to return the garden, and he told Thabit to take it and let her go. no villain, and a way out.

original.note: Arabic: release; in law, divorce by the husband.

trapdoor: what you thought: in Islam a man says one word three times and it's over.
what it means: divorce is permitted but disliked, with arbiters first, waiting periods, a way back, and parting in kindness. a wife can seek her release too.
what a scholar hears: talaq in revocable stages under 2:229, khul' from the wife of Thabit ibn Qays, and the schools' debate over three pronouncements at once.

sources.quoted: Divorce must be pronounced twice and then (a woman) must be retained in honour or released in kindness.

notes: Editor pass: teach now notes 2:229's exception to taking back the gift, which is the khul' case (old text said the verse forbids it outright, then told the khul' story); 'the idea runs through the verses' softened to 'some readers hear the same idea'; howItsDone 'often' changed to 'for example'.
2:229 quoted from Pickthall; confirm exact wording ('honour' is Pickthall's spelling).
Abu Dawud 2178: its chain is debated (some grade it weak or mursal); the script says so. Confirm.
Bukhari 5273 (khul'): her words paraphrased as 'afraid she'll fall short of what she owes in the marriage' for the report's 'I dislike kufr in Islam'; confirm this rendering.
'Each of those first two times, there is a waiting period, and during it the couple can come back together': confirm as a summary of revocable talaq.

Triple talaq in one sitting: mentioned only as a point where schools differ (the four Sunni schools traditionally count it as three; Ibn Taymiyya and some modern laws count it as one). Keeper may want more or less.
Day 632 (year 2) taught 65:1–2 and the 'iddah; this day uses 2:229, 4:35 and khul' to avoid repeating that angle.
